description: How DNA mutations create genetic variation, and why context decides if a change is harmful or not.
content_html:
What Is a Mutation?

The base sequence of DNA is not perfectly stable. Errors can arise when DNA is copied before cell division, or damage can be caused by environmental factors such as radiation or certain chemicals. A change to the base sequence of DNA is called a mutation. Mutations are the source of all new genetic variants — without them, there would be no variation between individuals of the same species.

There are three main types of mutation at the single-base level:

  • Substitution: one base is replaced by a different base (e.g. A replaced by C).
  • Insertion: an extra base is added into the sequence.
  • Deletion: a base is removed from the sequence.
Key Fact

Substitution mutations change only one codon (triplet). Insertion and deletion mutations shift the reading frame — every triplet after the mutation point is disrupted, potentially altering every amino acid from that point onwards in the protein chain.

Mutations in Coding DNA

If a mutation occurs in a coding region of DNA (within a gene), it may alter the amino acid sequence of the protein produced. There are three possible outcomes:

Harmful: the mutant protein folds incorrectly or cannot carry out its function. Enzymes may no longer catalyse their reaction; structural proteins may weaken tissues. Example: sickle cell disease, caused by a single base substitution in the gene for haemoglobin, which changes one amino acid and causes the protein to form rigid rods that distort red blood cells.

Neutral: the mutation either changes a codon to a synonymous codon (one that codes for the same amino acid — because the genetic code is redundant), or changes an amino acid in a region of the protein that is not critical to its function. The protein still works normally. Many mutations fall into this category.

Beneficial: rarely, a mutation produces a protein that functions better in particular conditions, or confers a survival advantage on the organism. Natural selection can then spread this variant through a population over many generations. Example: mutations giving bacteria resistance to an antibiotic are beneficial to the bacterium in an environment where that antibiotic is present.

Mutations in Non-Coding DNA

Not all mutations occur within genes. Large portions of the genome are non-coding DNA. These regions control whether genes are switched on or off — they regulate gene expression.

If a mutation occurs in a non-coding regulatory region, it does not alter the protein sequence directly. Instead, it alters the amount of protein produced, or when the gene is active. For instance, a mutation might silence a tumour-suppressor gene — the protein remains identical in structure, but the cell no longer produces enough of it to restrain cell division. This is one of the ways cancer can arise from mutations in non-coding regions rather than in the protein-coding sequence itself.

Key Fact

Mutations in non-coding DNA can affect phenotype by altering gene expression — changing how much of a protein is made, or whether it is made at all — without changing the protein’s structure. This means the same mutation can be harmful, neutral, or beneficial depending on the context: which gene is affected, in which tissue, and in what environment.

Context Determines Consequence

The same mutation can have entirely different consequences depending on context — a central idea in understanding genetic variation. The sickle cell allele, for example, is harmful when a person inherits two copies (causing sickle cell disease) but protective against severe malaria when only one copy is inherited. This explains why the allele remains common in populations from malaria-endemic regions: natural selection has maintained it because it confers a survival advantage in heterozygous individuals, even though it is harmful in homozygous form.

The environment plays a critical role in determining whether a mutation is disadvantageous. A mutation that impairs a metabolic pathway may be fatal in one nutritional environment but perfectly compatible with life in another where an alternative food source compensates. This interplay between genetic variant and environment underpins much of evolutionary biology and is central to understanding why genetic variation within a species is maintained rather than being eliminated by natural selection.

It is also important to remember that mutations occur randomly — they are not directed towards any goal. A bacterium does not develop antibiotic resistance because it ‘wants’ to survive; rather, random mutations arise all the time, and when an antibiotic is introduced, individuals that already carry a resistance mutation survive and reproduce while others die. The resistance spreads through natural selection, not through any purposeful change. This distinction between random mutation and directed adaptation is one of the most commonly misunderstood aspects of evolution.

Every person’s genome contains millions of single-base variants compared to any other person’s genome. The vast majority of these are neutral — they have accumulated over thousands of generations without affecting survival or reproduction. A small number influence disease risk, drug response, or physical characteristics. Modern genome sequencing allows scientists to identify which variants are associated with which outcomes — but association does not mean direct causation, and most complex traits involve hundreds of variants acting together.
exam_tip_html: When explaining the effect of an insertion or deletion mutation, use the term ‘frameshift’ and explain that all subsequent triplets are altered — this is the key difference from substitution, which only changes one codon. For questions asking you to evaluate whether a mutation is harmful, neutral or beneficial, always link to the context: a mutation that is harmful in one environment may be beneficial in another. Do not say mutations ‘always’ cause disease.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Mutations are changes to the DNA base sequence. Substitution changes one base; insertion adds a base; deletion removes a base. Insertions and deletions cause frameshifts, disrupting all subsequent codons.
  • Mutations in coding DNA may alter the amino acid sequence of a protein, potentially making it non-functional (harmful), unchanged in function (neutral), or better adapted (rarely, beneficial). The outcome depends on which amino acid is affected and whether it is in a critical region.
  • Mutations in non-coding regulatory DNA can change gene expression without altering the protein sequence itself. Whether a mutation is harmful, neutral or beneficial often depends on the environment and genetic context.

practice_questions.text: State the difference between a substitution mutation and an insertion mutation.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: substitution = one base replaced by a different base (one codon affected); insertion = an extra base added, causing a frameshift so all subsequent triplets are altered. Secure: both types described but frameshift not mentioned. Developing: one type described correctly. Emerging: vague reference to bases changing without specifying type.

practice_questions.text: Explain why an insertion mutation in a gene is likely to have a more severe effect on the protein produced than a substitution mutation.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: insertion causes a frameshift, shifting all subsequent triplets so every amino acid after the mutation point may be altered; substitution only changes one codon, so at most one amino acid changes; therefore insertion is more likely to disrupt protein function extensively. Secure: states frameshift disrupts subsequent codons; comparison to substitution included but mechanism less precise. Developing: states insertion changes more amino acids but does not explain frameshift mechanism. Emerging: vague statement that insertion is worse without reasoning.

practice_questions.text: Explain how a mutation in a non-coding region of DNA can affect an organism's phenotype.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: non-coding regions regulate gene expression; mutation may increase or decrease expression of a particular gene; this changes the amount of protein produced, altering the phenotype, even though the protein's sequence is unchanged. Secure: links non-coding DNA to gene regulation and altered protein levels; mechanism slightly vague. Developing: states non-coding DNA affects whether a gene is switched on but does not link to phenotype change clearly. Emerging: states non-coding DNA does not code for protein without further explanation.

practice_questions.text: The sickle cell allele causes disease when two copies are inherited but provides some protection against malaria when one copy is inherited. Use this example to explain how the same mutation can be beneficial, neutral or harmful depending on context.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: explains the allele is harmful in homozygous form (disease), protective in heterozygous form in malaria-endemic regions (benefit), and neutral in non-malaria regions; links to natural selection maintaining the allele where malaria is prevalent; draws the general principle that mutation consequence depends on genetic context and environment. Secure: explains both the harmful and beneficial aspects with reference to natural selection; general principle stated. Developing: describes the two outcomes but does not link to natural selection or general principle. Emerging: describes sickle cell disease correctly without addressing the context-dependence aspect.

practice_questions.text: A scientist studies a new gene variant in a population and finds it does not change the protein produced but is located in a regulatory region of DNA. Predict the likely effect on the organism, and justify your reasoning.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: predicts the variant could alter gene expression (increase or decrease when/how much protein is made); notes the protein structure is unchanged so function is unchanged; concludes the effect on phenotype depends on whether expression changes are significant in context; may be neutral (expression change too small to matter) or potentially harmful/beneficial if expression is dramatically altered. Secure: predicts altered gene expression and links to phenotype; justification present but lacks nuance about context. Developing: states regulatory region affects expression; limited prediction of outcome. Emerging: vague answer about non-coding DNA not being important.

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'genetic variant' and explain how genetic variants arise.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: a genetic variant is a different version of a gene (or allele); genetic variants arise from mutations (changes to the base sequence of DNA). Both points needed for full credit.

knowledge_checks.q: Which type of mutation is most likely to affect all amino acids after the mutation point?
Non-coding DNA is best described as DNA that:
options: Has no function in the cell
Controls gene expression rather than coding for proteins

knowledge_checks.q: A mutation that adds an extra base into the DNA sequence is called an _____.
A mutation in a regulatory (non-coding) region of DNA can affect phenotype by changing _____ expression.
Match each mutation type to its description.
right: A base is removed from the sequence
An extra base is added into the sequence
One base is replaced by a different base

flashcard_questions.a: A change in the base sequence of DNA.

flashcard_questions.q: What happens in a substitution mutation?
flashcard_questions.a: One base is replaced by a different base.

flashcard_questions.q: Why are insertion and deletion mutations more disruptive than substitution?
flashcard_questions.a: They cause a frameshift, altering every codon after the mutation point.

flashcard_questions.q: Give one example of a harmful mutation and name the disease it causes.
flashcard_questions.a: A base substitution in the haemoglobin gene causes sickle cell disease.
A mutation that does not change the function of the protein produced.
It regulates gene expression — controlling when and how much protein is made.

flashcard_questions.q: How can a mutation in non-coding DNA affect phenotype?
flashcard_questions.a: By altering gene expression without changing the protein's sequence.

flashcard_questions.q: Why can the same mutation be beneficial in one context and harmful in another?
flashcard_questions.a: Because the effect on survival depends on the environment and which copies of the allele are present.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the sickle cell allele's effect in heterozygous individuals in a malaria-endemic region?
flashcard_questions.a: It provides some protection against severe malaria.
The process by which a gene is read and its protein is produced.

flashcard_questions.q: Are most mutations harmful, neutral or beneficial?
Where do all genetic variants ultimately originate?
flashcard_questions.a: From mutations in the DNA base sequence.

glossary_terms.definition: A change in the base sequence of DNA. Mutations create new genetic variants and are the ultimate source of all genetic variation.
A mutation in which one base is replaced by a different base, changing a single codon.
A mutation in which an extra base is added into the DNA sequence, causing a frameshift from that point onwards.
A mutation in which a base is removed from the DNA sequence, causing a frameshift from that point onwards.
DNA sequences that contain the instructions for making a protein — the sections of a gene that are read and translated during protein synthesis.
DNA sequences that do not code for proteins but have regulatory roles, controlling when and how much specific genes are expressed.
The process by which the information in a gene is used to produce a functional protein. A gene is expressed when it is actively being read and its protein is being made.
